blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A pool class declares, in this order, `private final int capacity = 16 * factor();` and `private final int factor = Integer.getInteger("pool.factor", 4);`, where `factor()` returns the field `factor`. The property `pool.factor` is not set. What does `capacity` hold in a new pool?

options.text: 64, since the fields are all initialized before any of them is read
options.says: initializers run one after another in source order, so a method called from the first one reads the second field before its initializer has run

options.text: 0, since `factor` still holds its default value when the first initializer runs
options.says: capacity's initializer runs first; factor() reads the field, which is still 0, and Integer.getInteger is not a constant expression, so nothing is inlined

options.text: Nothing, since javac rejects a field initializer that reads a field declared below it
options.says: javac rejects naming a later field directly (illegal forward reference) but doesn't follow method calls, so this compiles

options.text: Nothing, since reading `factor` before its initializer has run throws a NullPointerException
options.says: an int field holds its default, 0, until its initializer runs; reading it is no error

origin.section: Spot the Problem: A Field Read Before Its Initializer Sees Its Default

questions.stem: `Widget`'s constructor does `label = caption();`, and `caption()` is abstract. `Button extends Widget` declares `private final String text = "Save";` and `private final String tooltip = "Save " + System.getProperty("doc", "draft");`, and implements `caption()` as `text + " / " + tooltip`. What is the `label` of a new `Button`?

options.text: "Save / Save draft", since a subclass's field initializers run before its superclass's constructor
options.says: the superclass constructor runs first; Button's initializers run only after it returns

options.text: "null / null", since neither of Button's fields has been assigned while Widget's constructor runs
options.says: text is a constant variable (final String with a constant initializer), so javac replaces its reads with "Save"

options.text: "Save / null", since only one of Button's fields is read from the object while Widget's constructor runs
options.says: text is a constant variable and is inlined; tooltip is not, and its field is still null when Widget's constructor calls caption()

options.text: No label, since a constructor that calls an abstract method of its own class doesn't compile
options.says: javac accepts the call; the override runs before the subclass is initialized, which is the bug

origin.section: Spot the Problem: A Field Read Before Its Initializer Sees Its Default

questions.stem: A `Dashboard` holds a 200 MB chart cache. Its instance method `start()` registers `new Listener() { public void onTick(Tick t) { redraw(t); } }` on a static `EventBus` that is never cleared; `redraw` is a `Dashboard` method. The user closes the dashboard, and the application drops every reference it had to it. What is still in memory after the next full collection?

options.text: The listener and the dashboard, since the listener keeps a reference to the dashboard
options.says: the anonymous class uses its outer instance (it calls an instance method), so javac gives it a this$0 field; the static bus keeps the listener, and through it the dashboard, reachable

options.text: The listener alone, since calling a dashboard method leaves no reference to the dashboard
options.says: calling an outer instance method uses the outer instance just as reading its field does, so the listener gets this$0

options.text: The listener alone, since nothing reachable keeps a reference to the dashboard
options.says: the listener's this$0 field refers to the dashboard, so the dashboard is reachable from the static bus

options.text: Neither of them, since the listener cannot outlive the dashboard that created it
options.says: the static bus refers to the listener, so it stays reachable after its creator is dropped, and its this$0 keeps the dashboard reachable too

origin.section: An Inner Class's Instance Holds Its Outer Object; a Static Nested Class's Doesn't

questions.stem: `Ledger.java` and `Statement.java` sit side by side, in no package, with no class files yet. `Ledger.java` declares `public class Ledger` and, below it, a package-private `class FeeSchedule`. `Statement` creates a `FeeSchedule`. What does `javac Statement.java`, run on its own, do?

options.text: It compiles, since a package-private class is visible to the other classes of its package
options.says: visibility is not the problem: javac has to find the class first, and it looks for it by name

options.text: It fails with `cannot find symbol`, since javac looks for `FeeSchedule` in a file of that name
options.says: javac finds a type it isn't compiling through FeeSchedule.class or FeeSchedule.java; neither exists, so the symbol is not found

options.text: It fails with an access error, since a second class in a file is private to that file
options.says: visibility isn't the problem: compiled together, both files build

options.text: It compiles, since javac reads the source files of the directory to find the classes it needs
options.says: javac looks a type up through a file named after it; the failing compile shows it does not find FeeSchedule inside Ledger.java

origin.section: A File Has at Most One Public Top-Level Class, and the File Is Named After It

concepts: javac 21 gives an inner or anonymous class the outer-instance field only when it uses the outer instance or is Serializable, and a lambda captures this only when it uses it.
A final field of primitive or String type initialized with a constant expression is a constant variable whose reads javac replaces with the value, so it never shows its default.
A field read before its initializer has run, through a method called from an earlier initializer, holds its default value; javac rejects only a direct forward reference.
Field initializers and instance initializer blocks run in source order, after the superclass constructor returns and before the rest of the constructor body.

A file holds at most one public top-level class, named after the file, and javac finds a type it isn't compiling by a file of that name, so a second top-level class is found only when its file is compiled with it.
